what_its_for: Probenecid helps your body get rid of extra uric acid through your urine. It is used to treat gout and gouty arthritis by lowering uric acid levels in your blood. It can also be used alongside certain antibiotics (like penicillin) to help them work better and stay in your body longer.
how_to_take: Take probenecid by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). You may take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Drink at least 6 to 8 full glasses of water or fluids every day while taking this medicine to help protect your kidneys and prevent kidney stones. Do not crush or chew the tablets unless your pharmacist says it is okay.
dosing: For gout, the usual starting dose is 250 mg (one-half tablet) taken twice a day for the first week. Your doctor will likely increase your dose to 500 mg (one tablet) twice a day after that. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time based on your uric acid levels. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first. Always take it exactly as prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next scheduled dose. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store probenecid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can raise uric acid levels and make your condition worse. Do not take aspirin or aspirin-containing products while on probenecid, as they can block how the medicine works — use acetaminophen (Tylenol) for pain relief instead unless your doctor says otherwise. Avoid foods high in purines (such as organ meats, anchovies, sardines, and shellfish) since these can raise uric acid. Talk to your doctor before starting any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements, as probenecid can interact with many drugs.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: signs of a kidney stone (severe back or side pain, blood in urine, painful urination); signs of an allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing); unusual bruising or bleeding; severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or a gout flare-up that is getting worse. Also call your doctor if you notice swelling, unusual tiredness, or any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Probenecid does not relieve a gout attack that has already started — it will not stop pain right away. It works slowly over weeks to months to lower uric acid levels and prevent future gout attacks. You may actually have more frequent gout flare-ups during the first few months of treatment as your body adjusts. This is normal. Do not stop taking the medicine — your doctor may prescribe another medicine to help with flare-ups during this time. Most people notice fewer gout attacks after 3 to 6 months of regular use.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Use with caution, as kidneys may not work as well with age, which can affect how this drug is removed from your body. Your doctor may adjust your dose. Kidney problems: This medicine may not work well if you have moderate to severe kidney disease. Tell your doctor if you have any kidney problems. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of probenecid in pregnancy is not fully established. Your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks for you. Children: Probenecid is sometimes used in children for antibiotic-related purposes. Dosing in children is based on weight and must be determined by a doctor.
